summary: The study holds one OpenAPI contract (the RealWorld/Conduit API) and one 291-assertion behavioral test suite fixed, then layers structural constraints on agents generating multi-file backends: Clean Architecture, a prescribed database (SQLite/PostgreSQL), and a prescribed ORM. The setting is 8 Python/Node frameworks, 2 scaffolds (Mini-SWE-Agent, OpenHands), and 8 models. Performance drops as constraints accumulate ('constraint decay'), with database and data-layer defects the dominant failure cause. 20 feature-implementation tasks carved out of real RealWorld repos show the difficulty persists in brownfield code.

claims.claim: Assertion pass rate drops ~27 pts on average from L0 (framework only) to L3 (arch+DB+ORM)
claims.evidence: Table 2 and §5.1. The abstract and contributions say 27.28 points, but the §5.1 body and takeaway say 27.48 pp, and Appendix D says 26 pp (no verifier) vs 27 pp (with verifier). The authors also say 'the variance of the drop across levels is substantial, so the precise effect size should be interpreted with caution'. The direction is robust across configurations; the exact number is not.

claims.claim: Specifying a database engine is the most damaging single constraint; ORM's marginal effect is small (and helps GPT-5.2)
claims.evidence: Table 3(a): matched-pair marginal deltas with ± stderr across all configurations.

claims.claim: Mid-tier models are framework-sensitive (Express/Koa/Flask ≫ Django/FastAPI/Hono); the gap mostly closes for strong models
claims.evidence: Figure 2 (± 1 s.e.): 43-69 pp spread for four mid-tier configs vs 16 pp (MiniMax-M2.5) and 21 pp (GPT-5.4); strong-model differences are mostly within stderr.

claims.claim: Data-layer defects cause ~48% of logic errors on average
claims.evidence: Table 4: GPT-5.2 judge over the last 20 turns, logs and test output. Validated against manual labels on 50 Qwen3-Coder-Next logic errors (κ=0.975), i.e. one model's failures only. 36.5-60.9% across models.

claims.claim: Decay is not an artifact of greenfield generation
claims.evidence: Table 3(b): 20 feature-implementation tasks ablated from RealWorld repos; only GPT-5.2 exceeds 50% pass@1 (GPT-5.2 single run). The authors concede structural constraints cannot be isolated as the cause here.

patterns.note: A machine-readable OpenAPI spec removes functional ambiguity and enables a framework-agnostic oracle, but writing more non-functional constraints into the spec lowers agent success. Specs alone do not make agents comply.
Explicit structural requirements are measurably harder to satisfy jointly; the ORM constraint occasionally reduces ambiguity (GPT-5.2).
Static architecture/DB/ORM verifiers catch structural non-compliance that behavioral tests miss (used as an eval gate; false-reject ≤0.5%, App. D). Not tested as in-loop feedback.
End-to-end HTTP behavioral tests (32 requests, 291 assertions) used as the oracle; agents could run the server but in-loop test feedback was not ablated.
Bash-only Mini-SWE-Agent vs tool-rich OpenHands: the winner is model-dependent, and OpenHands uses 12.9x more tokens for GPT-5-mini.
Reports ~4B tokens total and per-config token use (App. I); cost drove subset evaluation.
New constraint-layered backend benchmark (80 greenfield + 20 feature tasks).

methodology.sample: 80 greenfield tasks (10 constraint variants × 8 frameworks) + 20 feature tasks; one API contract; 3 trials per task-config; 3 configs on a 16-task subset (validated r=0.94 vs full set)
methodology.baselines: Within-study L0 vs L1-L3; no prior method baseline (not needed for a characterization study)
methodology.models: Devstral-Small, Qwen3-Coder-Next, Qwen3-235B-Instruct, MiniMax-M2.5, Kimi-K2.5, GPT-5-mini, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.4
methodology.variance: n=3 trials; ± stderr on marginal effects and framework plots; pass@k unbiased estimator
methodology.ablations: Per-constraint matched pairs; verifier on/off (App. D); scaffold comparison
methodology.contamination_controls: None. The API contract is the widely replicated RealWorld/Conduit spec with many public implementations, so L0 success may partly reflect memorisation.
methodology.languages: Python 3.12 (Flask, FastAPI, Django, aiohttp) and Node.js 20 (Express, Fastify, Hono, Koa); no Java/JVM

standards.artifacts: Pipeline, tasks, trajectories, analysis scripts at github.com/francdente/constraint-decay

biases.detail: The single API contract is RealWorld/Conduit; public implementations exist in every studied framework and the feature tasks are cut from those repos.
One functional specification, so 'task' variation is only constraint × framework.
The headline decay figure is inconsistent across sections (27.28 / 27.48 / 26-27 pp).
The failure-taxonomy judge (GPT-5.2) is validated only on 50 logic errors from one model; the other three models' labels are unvalidated.
Dynamic-language runtimes only; Spring/JPA/Hibernate are absent, though their convention-heavy design resembles the frameworks that hurt mid-tier models most.

coi.funding: EU Horizon Europe AI4SWEng (grant 101189909); French ANR 3IA Côte d'Azur (ANR-23-IACL-0001)
coi.detail: Independent academic evaluation; authors ship no evaluated system.

verdict_reason: A well-controlled design with 8 models, 2 scaffolds, 3 trials, matched-pair marginal effects, a verifier-impact audit and a subset-representativeness check, plus full artifacts. Caveats: a single, likely-contaminated API contract; no JVM frameworks; no main limitations section; and an inconsistent headline number (27.28 vs 27.48 pp).
applicability: Directly relevant to a Java backend team using spec-driven development. An OpenAPI contract plus behavioral HTTP tests is a good oracle, but adding architecture, database and ORM constraints to the spec makes agents worse, and data-layer code (queries, ORM usage) is where they fail. The team should (1) gate generated code with deterministic structural checks rather than trusting spec prose: ArchUnit-style layer rules, persistence-layer checks, Testcontainers-backed integration tests; (2) give agents existing repository and DAO exemplars instead of greenfield constraint lists; (3) expect worse results on convention-heavy stacks such as Spring/JPA. That last point is an inference from the Django/FastAPI results, since the paper tested no Java. With ingestion spanning several repositories, it helps to keep each repo's contract (OpenAPI/AsyncAPI) and its structural rules machine-checkable, so every agent host gets the same verdict.
